analysis.one_liner: Bans commercial asbestos nationwide, with a decade-long carve-out for chlorine plants.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in August 2026 and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, where it has received no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill writes a ban on commercial asbestos into the main federal toxics law, covering all known commercial asbestos types and any product made with it. It takes effect immediately on enactment, but it lets existing chlorine plants keep using asbestos until 2032 (2036 for some), lets asbestos sheet gaskets phase out under existing EPA deadlines, and allows presidential exemptions for national security. Metal ore mining is carved out entirely.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and the public: anyone exposed to asbestos fibers, which cause mesothelioma, lung cancer, and other fatal diseases. Under current law, chrysotile asbestos is still legally imported and used in a small number of chlorine plants, and asbestos-containing products can still be sold; this bill would end commercial manufacture, processing, use, and sale of asbestos and products containing it on the date of enactment.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and the public exposed to asbestos

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits any person from manufacturing, processing, using, or distributing in commerce commercial asbestos or any mixture or article containing it, effective on the date of enactment.

It covers all asbestiform varieties with commercial value — chrysotile, crocidolite, amosite, anthophyllite, tremolite, actinolite, richterite, and winchite — so the ban reaches beyond the one type (chrysotile) still imported today.
It removes the EPA's current regulatory pathway for asbestos use in chlorine plants and replaces it with a hard statutory end date, so the phase-out can no longer be extended administratively.

analysis.who_pays: Chlor-alkali producers that still use asbestos diaphragms to make chlorine and caustic soda, who would face conversion costs to alternative membrane technology, and the small set of importers and manufacturers of asbestos-containing products. Consumers could see modestly higher costs for chlorine-derived products during the transition.

drawbacks.text: Chlorine plants that were operating on enactment may keep using asbestos until May 25, 2032, and multi-facility companies that have been converting get an extension to May 25, 2036 — up to a decade of continued asbestos use at the country's remaining asbestos-dependent facilities.
Asbestos sheet gaskets are not banned outright; they remain subject to the existing EPA compliance dates instead of the immediate prohibition.

The President may exempt any person from the ban for national-security reasons for up to three years, extendable once, and may withhold publication of exemption information from the public if it would harm national security, reporting it only to two congressional committees.
Metal ore mining is entirely exempted, and the ban does not reach asbestos present 'solely as an impurity,' so trace contamination in other mined and processed materials stays outside the ban.

Asbestos already installed in buildings and equipment before enactment stays in place; the bill only excludes its end-use and disposal from the ban, meaning in-place asbestos exposure risks persist and must be handled through existing removal law.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health benefit is large and the bill is a real, immediate ban on commercial asbestos — the exposure risks that killed tens of thousands of Americans would end for all new uses. The main honest objection is the decade-long chlorine-plant carve-out, which delays the ban exactly where most remaining workers face routine exposure, and the sheet-gasket and impurity carve-outs leave some exposure pathways open. It is a strong bill with a negotiated softening, not a loophole-ridden one.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in early August 2026, read twice, and sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, where no further action has been taken and the Congress runs out in early January 2027.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the Alan Reinstein Ban Asbestos Now Act of 2026 in the Senate on August 4, 2026.
Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) joined as the bill's only cosponsor.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works; the action history shows no markup, hearing, or floor vote since referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one new: the status quo continues, in which chlorine plants keep using asbestos under EPA rules and asbestos-containing products remain on the market while the bill sits in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Chlorine plants and asbestos-product sellers, for now

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate and shepherded it through referral.

for.name: Sen. John Curtis
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the sole Republican supporter shown in the record.

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on August 4, 2026, and has taken no further action on it in the final months of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only Senate support on record is one Democrat (Merkley) and one Republican (Curtis); no member has opposed it on record because it has never received a markup or a vote.

industries.note: The bill bans asbestos everywhere else but lets these plants keep using asbestos diaphragms until 2032, or 2036 for multi-facility companies that have been converting, and precludes their compliance with the EPA's separate asbestos rules. The industry's interest in stretching out asbestos use runs against workers and nearby communities, but the carve-out does come with a hard statutory end date and interim exposure controls.

The bill ends manufacture, processing, use, and sale of asbestos-containing products immediately on enactment, except for sheet gaskets, which get existing EPA deadlines. Consumers and workers gain the removal of these products from commerce.

The bill expressly exempts extraction, beneficiation, and mineral processing of metal ores, so mining companies face no new liability for trace asbestos in ore. This carve-out poses little direct conflict with public health but narrows the ban's reach.

Asbestos already installed in buildings and equipment stays in place and remains subject to existing removal and disposal law, sustaining demand for licensed abatement work. Their interest in safe removal runs with the public's interest in getting asbestos out of buildings.

analysis.trajectory: The bill is a late-session introduction sitting in committee with no scheduled markup and no floor action, with only about five months left in this Congress. Bills at this stage — introduced in the final months, one sponsor, one cosponsor, no committee activity — almost never reach a vote; the realistic path is that it dies at the end of the 119th Congress and must be reintroduced in the next one, where prior versions of the Ban Asbestos Now Act have repeatedly stalled.
